YOUR MAP · SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS

What this KA covers

SWEBOK V4, Figure 1.1 — topics in the Software Requirements KA

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Why requirements
FROM WISHES TO ENGINEERING

Why do we specify at all?

Unspecified work

Building the wrong thing

Ambiguous goals · missed stakeholders · gold-plating · late discovery that “fast” meant two seconds, not two minutes.

Specified work

A testable contract

Agreement — what “done” means
Traceability — each feature points back to a need
Verification — a test can pass or fail it

The solution: requirements engineering defines WHO needs WHAT, WHY, and how we will know it was delivered.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Fundamentals
SWEBOK KA · FUNDAMENTALS

What counts as a requirement

IEEE / SWEBOK (three senses)

A user need · a capability the system must have · the documented representation of that need or capability.

Sommerville

Descriptions of the services a system should provide and the constraints on its operation and development.

Key artifact

The requirement

A condition or capability needed by a user to solve a problem or achieve an objective.

Understand the problem before solving it.

SWEBOK also splits product requirements (the software) from project requirements (how it will be built).

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Levels
TWO LEVELS OF DESCRIPTION

User requirements vs system requirements

User requirements

Natural language + diagrams for customers and end-users. Abstract. About goals.

System requirements

Detailed, often numbered, statements of services and constraints. Often contractual. For architects and developers.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.1 — one user need expanded into system requirements

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Audience
WHO READS WHAT

Different readers, different documents

Managers & clients

Need user-level statements they can accept or reject — not algorithms.

Engineers

Need system-level detail they can design, estimate, and test against.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.2 — readers of user vs system requirements

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · FR / NFR
FUNCTIONAL AND NON-FUNCTIONAL

What it does · how well it does it

Functional · FR

Services and behaviour

What the system should do in particular situations. Incomplete or inconsistent FRs are a classic project failure mode.

Non-functional · NFR

Quality and constraints

How well, how safe, how fast, under which rules. SWEBOK: technology constraints + quality of service. Often more critical than a single feature.

Year-1 rule: both kinds must be testable. “User-friendly” is not an NFR until you can measure it.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · FR examples
SIX DOMAINS, SAME PATTERN

Functional requirements: vague vs testable

DomainVague (wrong)Testable (right)
Reminders“The system should remind users.”If a task is open and due in 1 day, the system shall send a reminder.
Library loans“Users can borrow books easily.”If a member has <3 active loans, scanning a book shall register a 14-day loan.
Food delivery“The app shows order status.”When a rider marks “picked up”, the customer’s status shall update to “On the way” within 5 s.
Event RSVP“Users can RSVP to events.”Tapping “Going” before the deadline shall add the user to the attendee list and email confirmation within 1 min.
Attendance“The system tracks attendance.”Scanning an ID QR within 15 min of class start shall mark “Present”; after 15 min, “Late”.
Shopping cart“Users can manage their cart.”Setting an item’s quantity to 0 shall remove it and recalculate the total immediately.

Same fix every time: name the trigger (when/if), name the actor, and end with a number, a state, or a yes/no.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Three words, not one
DO NOT CONFUSE THESE THREE WORDS

Requirement ≠ Feature ≠ Backlog

RequirementFeatureBacklog
AnswersHow it must behave — testableWhat it does — a headlineWhat we do first / next
Detail levelDetailed, verifiableHigh-level summaryBroken into actionable tasks
Who uses this docSA, developers, QA — you, todayExecutives, customers, PMPO, the dev team

A Feature List is a table of contents. Your SRS today must go one level deeper — every FR must be testable, not just named.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · NFR types
PRODUCT · ORGANIZATIONAL · EXTERNAL

Types of non-functional requirements

Product

Usability, performance, dependability, security — properties of the software itself.

Organizational

Process, environment, and operational rules of the customer or the development team.

External

Law, regulation, ethics — including privacy / PDPA-style constraints.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.3 — classification of NFRs

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · NFR examples
SIX QUALITY ATTRIBUTES, SAME PATTERN

Non-functional requirements: vague vs measurable

AttributeVague (wrong)Measurable (right)
Performance“The system should be fast.”Dashboard shall load within 2 s on campus Wi-Fi, up to 200 concurrent users.
Security / Privacy“The system should keep data safe.”A user shall see only their own records; requesting another user’s ID directly shall return a 403 error.
Usability“The system should be user-friendly.”A first-time user shall finish sign-up in under 60 s without help.
Reliability“The system should be reliable.”The system shall be available 99% of the time, 08:00–18:00 on exam days, excluding planned maintenance.
Maintainability“The code should be easy to maintain.”A new FR shall be addable by changing ≤3 existing files, checked at code review.
Legal / PDPA“The system should follow privacy law.”The system shall get consent before storing personal data and delete it within 7 days of a deletion request.

Same fix as FR: swap the quality word (fast / safe / friendly / reliable) for a number, a rule, or a yes/no a test can check.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Metrics
IF YOU CANNOT MEASURE IT, YOU CANNOT ACCEPT IT

Metrics for specifying NFRs

Speed, size, reliability…

Sommerville’s table turns vague quality words into quantities: transactions per second, memory, mean time to failure, training time.

For StudyMate

Not “fast reminders” — within 1 minute of the scheduled time. Not “private” — a student sees only their own tasks.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.5 — example NFR metrics

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Metrics worked examples
ALL SIX PROPERTIES, FILLED IN

Same table, real numbers this time

PropertyMeasure (Sommerville)Worked example
SpeedResponse time, refresh rate, tx/sSearch results appear within 1.5 s of typing; dashboard refreshes every 5 s.
SizeMegabytes, payload sizeEach API response ≤200 KB; app first load ≤3 MB on mobile data.
Ease of useTraining time, help promptsA first-time user completes checkout in under 2 min with ≤1 tooltip.
ReliabilityMTTF, probability of unavailability, availabilitySystem available 99% of the time during exam week; MTTF ≥30 days.
RobustnessTime to restart, % events causing failureIf the payment API times out, the app retries once and shows an error within 3 s — it shall not crash.
Portability% target-dependent code, number of target systemsWeb app runs on Chrome, Safari, Edge unchanged; layout supported down to 360px width.

The property name tells you what to measure — Sommerville’s “Measure” column tells you the unit. Your job is the number.

discovering

SWEBOK wraps these as requirements development, and adds a parallel activity: requirements management (change control, scope, tracing).

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Development vs management
SWEBOK FIGURE 1.3

Development and management together

Development

Elicit → analyse → specify → validate. Produces the agreed requirements set.

Management

Scrubbing, change control, matching scope to budget. Requirements will change — the process must absorb that without chaos.

SWEBOK V4, Figure 1.3 — requirements activities

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Spiral
NOT A ONE-PASS PIPELINE

A spiral view of requirements engineering

Feasibility sits in the centre

Each loop revisits elicitation, specification, and validation. Early loops are coarse; later loops add precision.

Fits incremental SDLC

Week 2: you chose a process. This figure is how Specification actually repeats inside that process.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.12 — spiral model of RE

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Elicitation
ELICITATION AND ANALYSIS

A cycle, not a single interview

Discovery

Talk, observe, read documents. Needs vs wants.

Classification & organisation

Group, name, drop duplicates.

Prioritisation & negotiation

Stakeholders conflict. Someone decides.

Documentation

Write what was agreed — then loop again.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.13 — elicitation and analysis

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Techniques
HOW YOU DISCOVER

Elicitation techniques (year-1 set)

Interview

Last time it broke

Open and closed questions. Ask about goals and workarounds — not buttons.

Observation

Ethnography-lite

Watch the current system: LINE groups, paper lists, ignored alarms.

Stories & scenarios

A day in the life

Concrete episodes become user stories and, later, use cases (Week 4).

SWEBOK also lists prototypes, facilitated workshops, and models. Start with three reachable people from your M1 charter.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Specification
WAYS OF WRITING “SHALL”

Notations for system requirements

Natural language

Readable, but ambiguous. “The system shall load quickly.”

Structured NL / stories + AC

Year-1 choice: As a … I want … so that … plus Given/When/Then. SWEBOK: acceptance-criteria-based spec (ATDD/BDD family).

Graphical / mathematical

Use cases, models, formal specs — Week 4 for diagrams; not today’s main task.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.8 — ways of writing specifications

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Structured spec
WORKED EXAMPLE · NOT YOUR DOMAIN

A structured specification (insulin pump)

Why this figure

Function name, description, inputs, outputs, destination, requires, pre/post-conditions — a template that leaves nowhere to hide vagueness.

Your M2 equivalent

User story + two acceptance criteria is the lightweight form of the same idea.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.10 — structured NL specification

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · SRS
THE REQUIREMENTS DOCUMENT

Structure of an SRS — and our year-1 cut

Full IEEE-style document

Preface, introduction, glossary, user requirements, system architecture, system requirements, models, evolution, appendices, index.

M2 (this course)

Purpose & scope · stakeholders · FR as stories + AC · NFR including privacy · use-case names · out of scope · AI log. Diagrams next week.

Sommerville 9e, Figure 4.7 — requirements document structure

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Validation
CHECKS BEFORE YOU BUILD

Requirements validation

Validity

Right system?

Does this actually support the user’s real work?

Consistency · completeness

No clashes, no holes

Two FRs cannot contradict; nothing essential is missing.

Realism · verifiability

Can we build and test it?

Budget, skill, and a test that can fail the statement.

Techniques: reviews (your Week 5 cross-team R1), prototyping, generating tests from criteria. Reviews catch errors cheaper than code does.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Case study
APPLYING THEORY TO PRACTICE

Case study: StudyMate reminder

The project

A student tool that stores tasks and reminds before deadlines. Teaching demo only — not your assignment domain.

The challenge

Turn “don’t let me submit late” into FR + NFR a test can check.

Context

Personal data, an optional AI parser, and a small Year-1 team using incremental development.

StudyMate · FR-3

Remind · only if open · only mine

FR: reminder 1 day before an open task. NFR-2: within 1 minute. NFR-5: a student sees only their own tasks.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · One FR, one small picture
ONE FR, ONE SMALL DIAGRAM — NOT UML YET

See the requirement as a picture

The same FR-3 story has two acceptance criteria. Drawn as a flow, they are two paths — this is the shape a use-case/activity diagram will take in Week 4.

Task is open
1 day before due
→
System reminds
AC1 — testable
Task marked done
any time
→
Stays silent
AC2 — testable

Draw your own FR the same way tonight — two boxes and an arrow is enough. If you cannot draw it, the AC is probably still vague.
Shift-left: the AC you write today is the test, moved to day one — cheaper than finding the same bug in Week 7, and it forces the whole team to agree on “done” now, not later.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · A prompt is a spec too
A PROMPT IS A SPEC TOO

Vague prompt in → vague requirement out

Vague prompt

“Write the requirements for our coffee ordering system.”

No role, no context, no constraint, no output shape — AI fills the gaps by guessing, same as a vague user story.

Prompt with context

“You are a business analyst. From this interview note [pasted], draft one FR about drink customisation. Include a number or a state — no ‘easy’ or ‘fast’.”

→ FR: “When a customer selects a hot/iced/blended drink, the system shall show 4 sweetness levels (0/25/50/100%), default 100%.” (testable)

Same failure mode both ways: missing context → vague output. Feed AI the real interview note, not a one-line wish, before you ask it to draft.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Spec & V&V
CLOSING THE LOOP

From vague idea to verified product

Applying specification · the what

Bad spec: “As a user, I want the system to load very quickly, so that I feel satisfied.” (too vague)

Good spec: “As a student, I want a reminder 1 day before an open deadline so I submit on time.” + AC: open → remind; done → silent. (testable)

Applying validation · the check

Unit test (Week 7): does tasks_due_for_reminder return only open tasks 1 day away?

User validation: do students actually act on the reminder, or dismiss it like a phone alarm?

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Key points
TAKEAWAYS · THEN STUDIO

What to remember

A requirement is a testable contract, not a wish.
User vs system · FR vs NFR · product vs project — know which box you are in.
Elicit → analyse → specify → validate, then manage change. It spirals.
Year-1 notation: user stories + acceptance criteria. UML pictures are Week 4.
AI may draft. You verify against a real stakeholder and a future test.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Studio
STUDIO · 13:40–14:35

From interview to a contract

A · 15 min

Role-play

Pain, workaround, data you must never collect.

B · 25 min

Write in the .docx

3–5 FRs with AC. Stay inside your M1 MVP.

C · 10 min

Scope freeze

In-MVP box and Out box. More than 5 FRs → cut.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Roles
STATION A · FIVE HATS

Do not open with “we will build an app…”

1

Primary user

Answer from memory.

2

Other stakeholder

Admin, shop, instructor…

3

Analyst

Questions only.

4

Privacy

Can we store this?

5

Scribe

Pain · workaround · ban.

Start: Tell me about the last time this problem actually happened. Walking questions: How do you know? Evidence or assumption?

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Quality gates
STATION B · EACH STORY IN THE TEMPLATE

Four boxes or it does not count

Role is not the word “user”
There is a “so that …” benefit tied to interview pain
At least two acceptance criteria a test could fail
No quickly / easy / smart / user-friendly — put a number or yes/no

AI may draft five stories. You keep three, fix every line, and log the prompt in section 8 of the template.

▶ intro2se-w3-req.fig · Critique #3
AI CRITIQUE #3 · 10 MINUTES · A4

Spot it. Explain. Fix it.

AI-generated user story

As a user, I want the system to load data very quickly, so that I feel satisfied.

Name the error (vague / not measurable). Say why a test cannot use it. Rewrite with a number. No paper = no attendance mark.
